newsitem.title: CHINA: FORECAST - Chinese yuan to appreciate on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Chinese yuan to appreciate on Hong Kong.

text.p: The Chinese yuan is likely to appreciate against the U.S. dollar in the next few weeks with the conclusion of the Hong Kong handover reducing the need of the central bank to buy dollars, analysts said on Friday.

Analysts said one of the reasons China had pushed its foreign exchange reserves so high over the past year was to create a war chest of cash to deal with any problems stemming from the resumption of Chinese control over Hong Kong.

With the transition so far progressing smoothly since Chinese resumed control of the territory at midnight on Monday, and foreign exchange reserves now over $115 billion, the central bank can take a rest, they said.

"The Chinese yuan is likely to go steadily up against the U.S. dollar in the next few months following Hong Kong's return," said a banker who trades on the Shanghai-based national foreign exchange interbank market.
"The market widely expects the central bank to reduce its intervention in the market and buy less dollars," he added.

"The dollar-buying was partly the result of government concerns over possible foreign exchange needs during Hong Kong's transition. Now the takeover is over, the central bank is expected to reduce its activity in the market," a second local banker said.

A European banker in Hong Kong said maintaining the stability of the Hong Kong financial system and the Hong Kong dollar was now a prime concern of the Chinese central bank, the People's Bank of China.

"They are aware of the possibility of some unexpected event hitting the Hong Kong dollar, and they want to be prepared to defend it if necessary, which was one of the main reasons for them building the foreign reserves," the banker said.
"Another reason was pure financial machismo," he added.

Intervention by the central bank on the foreign exchange market, buying dollars to keep the yuan down and to build the reserves, has been a significant market factor, but has dropped off markedly in recent weeks, dealers say.
"The bank used to intervene in the markets at least two or three times a week to prevent the yuan rising, but it has only done so once since the start of last month," a second trader said.
"It's an indication of how the central bank is gradually reducing its activity," he said.
The yuan ended up 8.2915 against the dollar on Friday from Thursday's 8.2930 on the Shanghai-based China Foreign Exchange Trade System, an interbank market.

Some analysts said they believed the yuan could push through a two-year high close of 8.2892 set on May 18, 1995 over the next few weeks, but added that the currency's rise will continue to be slow and steady.

"The central bank doesn't want the yuan to devalue, although that would please the exporters, and it doesn't want it to rise much beyond its current level," said the European banker. "Its top priority is to keep the yuan stable."

The Chinese yuan has been on a glacially-slow upward trend since the Shanghai-based interbank market was launched in 1994 due to China's rising foreign exchange reserves and a heavy foreign trade surplus, analysts said.
It has been one of the world's most stable currencies in recent years. It rose 0.3 percent against the dollar in 1996 after a rise of 2.9 percent in 1994 and 1.5 percent in 1995.
